disclaimer: Independent vendor-neutral practice material by Interstitium Labs. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by any vendor. Confers no certificate. All scenarios are original.

scenarios.title: SLI, SLO, SLA — untangled
scenarios.situation: A contract promises customers 99.9% uptime with credits if breached. Internally, the team targets 99.95% and measures 'successful requests / total requests' monthly.
scenarios.prompt: Label each: which is the SLI, the SLO, and the SLA?
choices: SLI: the measured ratio of successful requests; SLO: the internal 99.95% target; SLA: the contractual 99.9% promise with credits
SLI: 99.9%; SLO: the credit policy; SLA: the measurement query
They're synonyms — pick whichever term the customer prefers
SLI: the contract; SLO: the measurement; SLA: the internal target
scenarios.why: SLI (indicator) is the measurement — what you actually quantify. SLO (objective) is the internal target you aim for, set tighter than any contract. SLA (agreement) is the external commitment with consequences. Keeping SLO > SLA gives you a buffer: you can miss the SLO and still honor the SLA.
scenarios.hint: Which one is a number you measure, which is a goal you set, which is a promise you sign?

scenarios.title: How much downtime is 99.9%?
scenarios.situation: Your SLO is 99.9% monthly availability. Product wants to know exactly how much downtime that allows before the error budget is blown.
scenarios.prompt: What is the monthly error budget, and what does exhausting it imply?
choices: About 43 minutes — 0.1% of ~43,200 minutes/month; exhausting it should freeze risky releases until the budget recovers
About 7 hours — 1% of a 30-day month
About 4 minutes — 99.9% leaves almost no room
It depends on traffic — downtime can't be computed from a percentage
scenarios.why: Error budget = 1 − SLO = 0.1% of the window. A 30-day month ≈ 43,200 minutes; 0.1% ≈ 43.2 minutes. The budget is a policy tool: while budget remains, teams may take release risks; when it's exhausted, the deal is to prioritize reliability work over features until it recovers. That's the core SRE bargain.
scenarios.hint: What is 0.1% of 43,200 minutes?

scenarios.title: Fast burn at 3 AM
scenarios.situation: Your error budget burns at 14x the sustainable rate — at this pace the monthly budget is gone in ~2 days. The alert fired 10 minutes ago. A slower alert would have fired in 6 hours at 2x burn.
scenarios.prompt: How should burn-rate alerting treat these two cases differently?
choices: Fast burn pages immediately (urgent, budget-exhausting); slow burn opens a ticket for business hours (needs attention but not a page)
Both should page — any burn above 1x is an emergency
Neither should page — budgets are monthly, so wait until month end
Page on slow burn only — fast burn resolves itself
scenarios.why: Multiwindow burn-rate alerting distinguishes urgency: fast burn (e.g., 14x over 1h/5m windows) exhausts budget in days → page now. Slow burn (e.g., 2–6x over longer windows) exhausts in weeks → ticket for investigation during work hours. This is how you page on user-impacting budget consumption without alert fatigue.
scenarios.hint: How quickly does each burn rate consume the monthly budget?

scenarios.title: The vanity SLI
scenarios.situation: The team proposes 'CPU utilization below 70%' as an SLI with a 95% SLO. The dashboard is green while users complain the checkout is slow.
scenarios.prompt: Why is this a bad SLI, and what should replace it?
choices: CPU doesn't measure user experience — SLIs should capture what users feel: request success rate and latency percentiles at the service edge
CPU is hard to measure — pick something easier like disk space
The threshold is wrong — 70% should be 90%
SLIs must be infrastructure metrics — user metrics belong in product analytics
scenarios.why: Good SLIs measure user-visible outcomes (availability, latency, correctness, throughput) as experienced at the service boundary — not internal resource gauges that can look healthy during an outage. Latency percentiles (p95/p99) and success ratios on real user journeys are the canonical choices; CPU is at best a supporting signal.
scenarios.hint: Can a user tell what your CPU utilization is?

scenarios.title: Budget exhausted — now what?
scenarios.situation: The team burned the entire error budget by the 12th of the month after three risky launches. Product still wants two more feature launches this month.
scenarios.prompt: What does the error-budget policy say, and why does the deal work?
choices: Freeze feature launches and spend remaining capacity on reliability work — the deal works because both sides agreed to the budget rules in advance
Keep launching — budgets are advisory and product decides
Lower the SLO retroactively so the budget isn't exhausted
Blame the on-call engineer for the incidents
scenarios.why: The error budget is a joint policy: product gets launch velocity while budget remains; engineering gets reliability investment when it's gone. It works because it's agreed upfront, data-driven (not political), and symmetric — it protects launches when reliability is good too. Retroactively moving the SLO destroys trust in the whole system.
scenarios.hint: What was agreed before the month started about an exhausted budget?

scenarios.title: Forty-seven SLOs
scenarios.situation: Every microservice team defined 5–6 SLOs. Nobody can say which ones matter; alerts fire constantly and get ignored.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Consolidate on a few user-journey SLOs per critical path — fewer, meaningful SLOs that people actually honor beat dozens that everyone ignores
Add more SLOs so every metric is covered
Raise all thresholds to 99.99% so alerts fire less
Delete SLOs entirely and rely on uptime pings
scenarios.why: SLOs are attention-directing instruments: each one implies alerting, policy, and on-call burden. A handful of SLOs on critical user journeys (checkout works, search is fast) that the org genuinely defends beats a sprawling catalog nobody trusts. Unused SLOs are worse than none — they train people to ignore the system.
scenarios.hint: If everything is critical, what is?

choices: CPU utilization measures resource usage, not user experience — a good SLI quantifies what users feel (request success rate, latency percentiles), because the SLO exists to protect users, not servers
70% is too high; the SLO should be < 50% to be safe
Average is wrong; they should use the maximum CPU across the fleet
SLIs must be defined by the infrastructure team, not the service team
scenarios.hint: If this SLI is green but every user request fails, what has the SLO actually protected?
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this SLI?
scenarios.situation: A team defines their SLI as 'average CPU utilization across the fleet' with an SLO of '< 70%'.
scenarios.title: Picking a Good SLI
scenarios.why: SLIs must reflect the user's experience of the service: proportion of successful requests, latency of successful requests, freshness of data. Resource metrics are useful for capacity planning and alerting internals, but a service can be at 40% CPU and completely broken (or 95% CPU and perfectly healthy). SLOs on the wrong signal drive the wrong behavior.

choices: Freeze non-urgent feature releases and focus on reliability work until the budget recovers — the error budget is the agreed trade-off mechanism: budget spent means reliability work takes priority over features
Ship anyway; SLOs are aspirational and budgets reset monthly
Lower the SLO to 99% so the budget is no longer exhausted
Exclude the bad deploy's errors from the SLI retroactively
evidence:
Error budget: 43.2 min/month
Consumed by day 10: 43.2 min (100%)
scenarios.hint: The budget is a deal made in advance between product and engineering. What was the deal?
scenarios.prompt: What does the error-budget policy dictate?
scenarios.situation: The checkout service has a 99.9% SLO (43 min/month error budget). It's the 10th and the budget is fully burned after a bad deploy. Product wants to ship a big feature on the 12th.
scenarios.title: Error Budget Exhausted
scenarios.why: The error budget makes the reliability/feature trade-off explicit and pre-negotiated: as long as budget remains, ship fast; when it's gone, reliability work wins. That's the entire point — decisions during calm times, not arguments during incidents. Retroactively editing the SLI or lowering the SLO to dodge the policy destroys trust in the system.

choices: Use multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts (e.g., Google's SRE workbook pattern: fast-burn 1h/5m windows for paging, slow-burn 6h/30m for tickets) tied to the error budget — fast burns page, slow burns ticket, and both reset correctly
Lower the threshold to 0.1% so the slow burn would have paged
Raise the `for:` duration to 1 hour to stop the noisy pages
Alert on total error count instead of ratio; ratios hide slow burns
evidence: 0.4% errors for 6h = budget exhausted, never paged
scenarios.hint: You need two different urgencies: 'budget burning fast, wake someone' and 'budget leaking slowly, file a ticket'. How many thresholds does that need?
scenarios.prompt: What alerting design fixes both failure modes?
scenarios.situation: The team pages on 'error rate > 1% for 5 minutes'. They get paged for brief spikes that self-resolve, and once missed a slow burn that exhausted the budget over 6 hours without ever tripping the alert.
scenarios.title: Multi-Window Burn Alerts
scenarios.why: Single-threshold alerts can't distinguish a 5-minute spike from a 6-hour bleed. Burn-rate alerting ties directly to the SLO: the fast-burn alert catches budget consumption at 14.4x+ (page-worthy), the slow-burn catches 6x+ over long windows (ticket-worthy). Both use paired long/short windows so alerts reset promptly when the burn stops, avoiding flapping.

scenarios.title: Is this a SEV-1?
scenarios.situation: Checkout is down for all users (revenue impact), but the status page still shows green because the SEV wasn't declared. Engineers are debugging in a side thread with no coordination.
scenarios.prompt: What should happen in the first 10 minutes?
choices: Declare the incident with a severity, page the on-call, establish an incident commander and a comms channel — coordination before heroics
Keep debugging quietly — declaring incidents creates paperwork
Wait for the monitoring to auto-declare — humans shouldn't declare
Fix it first, then decide if it was a SEV
scenarios.why: Declaring early is cheap and reversible; declaring late costs coordination. SEV levels (e.g., SEV-1 = critical user/business impact) set response urgency. The incident commander coordinates (not necessarily the fixer), comms owns status updates — this structure prevents 15 people debugging the same thing blind.
scenarios.hint: What costs more: a false-alarm declaration, or 30 minutes of uncoordinated debugging?

scenarios.title: Too many cooks
scenarios.situation: During an outage, six engineers are all SSHing into prod, running conflicting commands — one restarts the DB while another is mid-diagnosis on it.
scenarios.prompt: Which incident role fixes this, and how?
choices: The Incident Commander — single decision-maker who coordinates actions, tracks state, and keeps everyone else from stepping on each other
More engineers — the problem is understaffing
The most senior engineer should just fix it alone
Disable SSH for everyone except one person permanently
scenarios.why: The IC's job is coordination, not fixing: maintain shared state (what we know, what we're trying), serialize high-risk actions, and manage comms. Responders propose actions; the IC approves and sequences them. This is why 'all hands on keyboards' without an IC makes outages longer, not shorter.
scenarios.hint: Who decides what happens next when everyone disagrees?

scenarios.title: The deploy that broke prod
scenarios.situation: Ana's deploy caused a 40-minute outage. The postmortem draft says 'Root cause: Ana deployed without checking the dashboard.'
scenarios.prompt: Why is this postmortem framing harmful, and what replaces it?
choices: It blames the person instead of the system — rewrite around 'how did our process allow an unchecked deploy to reach prod' with systemic action items
It's accurate — accountability means naming who caused it
Skip the postmortem — the fix is to tell Ana to be careful
Blameless means no action items — just move on
scenarios.why: Blameless postmortems assume people act reasonably given their context; failures reveal system gaps (missing deploy gates, no canary, unclear dashboards). 'Be more careful' isn't an action item — 'add a pre-deploy checklist gate in CI, owner + date' is. Blame drives incidents underground; systems thinking prevents recurrence.
scenarios.hint: If Ana left tomorrow, would the same outage be possible?

scenarios.title: The runbook from 2019
scenarios.situation: The 'database failover' runbook references servers decommissioned in 2021 and commands for a version two majors old. On-call engineers ignore runbooks entirely now.
scenarios.prompt: What makes a runbook trustworthy?
choices: Tested regularly (game days), version-controlled with the service, with preconditions, exact commands, expected outputs, and rollback steps — owned by someone
Longer runbooks — detail equals quality
Runbooks written once by the original author and never touched
Replace runbooks with a Slack channel — docs are obsolete
scenarios.why: A runbook is production code for humans: it rots like code. Trust comes from regular testing (chaos/game days), co-versioning with the service it covers, clear preconditions ('only if X'), copy-pasteable commands with expected output, and an explicit owner. Untrusted runbooks are worse than none — they waste incident time.
scenarios.hint: When was the last time anyone verified these steps work?

scenarios.title: Silence during the outage
scenarios.situation: The outage lasts 2 hours. Engineering is heads-down fixing; customers hear nothing until the all-clear. Support is flooded with 'is it down?' tickets.
scenarios.prompt: What comms discipline was missing?
choices: A dedicated comms lead posting regular status updates (e.g., every 15–30 min) on the status page — even 'still investigating' beats silence
Faster fixing — comms don't matter if you fix quickly
Only the CEO should communicate during incidents
Post-mortems replace status updates
scenarios.why: Separate the comms role from the fixers: stakeholders need predictable updates (impact, what's being done, next update time) on a cadence, starting within minutes. Silence breeds speculation and duplicate tickets. 'No new information' is itself an update — it tells people the situation is being worked, not ignored.
scenarios.hint: What do customers assume when they hear nothing for an hour?

scenarios.title: Pager burnout
scenarios.situation: The on-call engineer got paged 31 times last week, mostly for non-urgent issues and flapping alerts. They're threatening to quit the rotation.
scenarios.prompt: What are the systemic fixes?
choices: Page only on urgent, actionable, user-impacting conditions; tune or ticket the rest; track paging load per person and compensate rotations
Pay the engineer more — burnout is a compensation problem
Rotate faster — daily rotations spread the pain
Mute the pager — alerts are optional
scenarios.why: Pager health is a reliability input: every page should be urgent (needs a human now), actionable, and ideally user-impacting — everything else becomes a ticket or gets fixed/tuned. Track pages per on-call shift; sustained overload means the alerting needs work, not the engineer. Google's SRE guidance treats excessive paging as a bug in the system.
scenarios.hint: Which of those 31 pages truly needed a human at 3 AM?

choices: Establish command: declare the incident, assign roles (commander, communications, ops), set a coordination rhythm — parallel uncoordinated debugging wastes the critical first minutes and leaves stakeholders blind
Let the most senior engineer debug alone; too many cooks spoil the incident
Immediately roll back the last deploy; action beats process
Wait 15 minutes to see if monitoring self-resolves before declaring
scenarios.hint: Five people debugging five theories with no updates — what role is missing?
scenarios.prompt: What is the incident commander's first move?
scenarios.situation: The payments API is down. Five engineers are in the incident channel, all debugging different theories, and nobody is updating the status page.
scenarios.title: Incident Commander First Move
scenarios.why: The first minutes of an incident are a coordination problem, not a technical one. Declaring the incident and assigning roles (who debugs, who communicates, who tracks time) converts chaos into parallel productive work and ensures stakeholders get updates. Blind rollback without diagnosis can worsen things; waiting wastes the golden window.

choices: Blame fixes nothing: the system allowed a single command to cause an outage, so the action items must address systemic causes (guardrails, confirmations, dry-run modes, blast-radius limits) — blameless postmortems keep people honest, and honesty is what finds real root causes
The engineer should be named so others learn from the example
'Be more careful' is sufficient; most outages are human error
Skip the postmortem; the cause is obvious
scenarios.hint: If a careful, well-rested engineer could still make this mistake tomorrow, what have you actually fixed by naming them?
scenarios.prompt: Why is this the wrong response, and what should replace it?
scenarios.situation: After an outage caused by an engineer running a destructive command, a manager wants the postmortem to name the engineer and add 'be more careful' as the action item.
scenarios.title: Blameless Postmortem Pushback
scenarios.why: Human error is never the root cause — it's the starting point. If one mistyped command can take down production, the system is fragile by design: missing confirmations, no dry-run, excessive privileges, no canary. Blame drives incidents underground (people hide mistakes), while blameless analysis surfaces the systemic fixes that prevent entire classes of failure.

scenarios.title: Which pillar for which question?
scenarios.situation: Three questions: (1) 'Is error rate elevated right now?' (2) 'What did the failing request do step by step?' (3) 'Show me one slow request's journey across 5 services.'
scenarios.prompt: Map each to metrics, logs, or traces.
choices: Metrics → (1) real-time aggregates and alerting; Logs → (2) discrete event detail; Traces → (3) cross-service request journey
Logs answer all three — metrics and traces are redundant
Metrics → (3), Traces → (1), Logs → (2)
Only APM vendors provide these — open source can't
scenarios.why: Metrics are aggregated numbers over time (rates, percentiles) — ideal for dashboards and alerts. Logs are discrete timestamped events with context — ideal for 'what happened' forensics. Traces follow one request across service boundaries via spans — ideal for latency attribution. Mature observability correlates all three (exemplars link metrics to traces, trace IDs in logs).
scenarios.hint: Which signal aggregates, which narrates, and which follows a request?

scenarios.title: The metric that ate Prometheus
scenarios.situation: Someone adds user_id as a Prometheus label on http_requests_total. With 2M users, Prometheus OOMs within an hour.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong, and what's the rule for labels?
choices: Label cardinality explosion — every unique label combination is a new time series; keep labels to bounded dimensions (method, status, endpoint), never unbounded IDs
Prometheus can't handle 2M series — use fewer metrics
Labels are free — the OOM is a Prometheus bug
user_id is required — buy a bigger server
scenarios.why: Prometheus stores one time series per unique label set — 2M user_ids × methods × statuses = tens of millions of series, each with memory/index cost. Rule: labels must be bounded, low-cardinality dimensions. High-cardinality identifiers belong in logs/traces (or exemplars linking a metric series to trace IDs), not metric labels.
scenarios.hint: What does each unique label value multiply?

scenarios.title: USE vs RED
scenarios.situation: You're building dashboards for (a) a Kubernetes node and (b) the checkout API service. Someone suggests the same dashboard template for both.
scenarios.prompt: Which method fits each, and why?
choices: USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) for the node/resource; RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) for the request-driven service
RED for both — USE is deprecated
USE for both — services are resources too
Neither — dashboards should be ad hoc
scenarios.why: USE targets resources: how full (utilization), how queued (saturation), error counts. RED targets services: request rate, error rate, duration (latency distribution). Node dashboards get CPU/memory/disk-queue panels; service dashboards get RPS, error %, p50/p95/p99 latency. The four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) blend both views.
scenarios.hint: Is a node more like a resource or a request-driven service?

scenarios.title: The alert nobody acts on
scenarios.situation: 'CPU above 80% for 5m' pages weekly. Every time, the responder looks, sees nothing wrong, and goes back to sleep. It's now muted — along with, people fear, something important.
scenarios.prompt: What makes an alert pageable vs ticket-worthy?
choices: Page only when it's urgent, actionable, and user-impacting (or budget-burning); 'CPU 80%' is a symptom-free threshold — alert on the SLO/burn rate instead, ticket the CPU trend
Lower the threshold to 60% — earlier pages catch more
Page on everything — muting is the real problem
Delete all CPU alerts — CPU never matters
scenarios.why: Every page should pass: does a human need to act NOW, and is there something they CAN do? Symptom-based alerting (error budget burn, latency SLO breach) pages; cause-based signals (CPU trend, disk growth) become tickets/dashboards. Alert fatigue is a reliability bug — each ignored page trains the team to ignore the next real one.
scenarios.hint: At 3 AM, what would the responder actually DO about 'CPU 80%'?

scenarios.title: Too many logs, too much money
scenarios.situation: Debug-level logs from 500 Pods cost $40k/month in ingestion. Dropping to error-only loses the context needed for debugging.
scenarios.prompt: What are the principled options?
choices: Structured info-level by default, dynamic debug toggling, tail-based trace sampling, and dropping noisy health-check logs at the collector
Log everything — observability has no cost ceiling
Delete logs older than 1 hour — recency is all that matters
Turn off logging in production — metrics suffice
scenarios.why: Cost control without blindness: log at info in prod (debug behind a runtime toggle for incidents), sample traces tail-based (keep the interesting ones — errors, slow), filter known-noise at the collector (kube-probe 200s), and set retention tiers (hot 7d, cold archive). Logging is a budget line item to manage, not an unlimited tap.
scenarios.hint: Which logs do you actually need when nothing is wrong?

scenarios.title: Dashboard for the error budget
scenarios.situation: Leadership wants 'a reliability dashboard'. The team proposes 40 graphs of CPU, memory, and network per service.
scenarios.prompt: What should the top-level reliability dashboard actually show?
choices: Per-service SLO compliance, error budget remaining + burn rate, and the golden signals — business-relevant reliability first, infra metrics one click down
40 infra graphs — more data is more reliable
Only uptime percentages — one number suffices
Dashboards are vanity — skip them
scenarios.why: The reliability dashboard answers 'are we meeting our promises and how fast are we consuming the budget': SLO status per user journey, budget remaining, burn-rate trend, annotated with deploys/incidents. Infra metrics support diagnosis but don't belong at the top — nobody's promise to customers is 'CPU under 70%'.
scenarios.hint: What question does leadership actually need answered?

scenarios.title: The cardinality explosion
scenarios.situation: Prometheus is OOMing after a deploy added user_id as a metric label. Ingestion lag is growing; queries time out.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct fix?
choices: Remove user_id from labels (keep bounded labels like endpoint/status); move per-user detail to logs/traces
Vertically scale Prometheus (more RAM)
Shard Prometheus by user_id hash
Drop the metric entirely
scenarios.hint: Which label has unbounded values?
scenarios.why: The 4.2M series come from the unbounded user_id label — each user multiplies every other label combination. Removing it collapses the series count to the bounded set (endpoints × statuses), and per-user questions move to logs/traces where high cardinality is fine. Choice 2 feeds the explosion. Choice 3 is complex machinery preserving a bad design. Choice 4 loses the SLI signal. Correct: bounded labels; high-cardinality detail in logs/traces.

scenarios.title: How much headroom?
scenarios.situation: The checkout service runs at 75% CPU at peak. Traffic grows 8% monthly. Finance asks whether you need new capacity this quarter.
scenarios.prompt: How do you do the capacity math?
choices: Project growth to peak, keep N+1 headroom (survive one zone/node failure), and trigger provisioning before utilization hits the danger zone — not after
Run at 100% — headroom is waste
Buy 10x capacity — growth is unpredictable
Capacity planning is guesswork — skip it
scenarios.why: Capacity planning: model peak (not average) load, project growth, maintain headroom for failure (N+1: full load sustainable minus one failure domain) and for deploy/rollout overhead. Provision on leading indicators (trend crossing threshold in X weeks), because procurement/provisioning has lead time. Autoscaling handles variance; planning handles the baseline.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the 75%-utilized service when one zone fails?

scenarios.title: What kind of load test?
scenarios.situation: You need to (a) validate the SLO at expected peak, (b) find the breaking point, (c) check for slow leaks over time.
scenarios.prompt: Which test types map to each goal?
choices: Load test (a — expected peak), stress test (b — beyond peak to failure), soak test (c — sustained load for hours/days)
One test covers all three — types are marketing
Spike test for (a), load for (b), stress for (c)
Load testing is only for launches — skip it otherwise
scenarios.why: Load: expected-peak traffic, validates SLOs under normal extremes. Stress: push past peak to find the breaking point and observe failure mode (graceful degradation?). Soak: moderate load for extended time to catch leaks (memory, connections, disk). Spike: sudden surges (flash sales). Run in prod-like envs; never surprise-test prod without coordination.
scenarios.hint: Which test finds the breaking point, and which finds the slow leak?

scenarios.title: HPA isn't saving us
scenarios.situation: The HPA scales Pods on CPU, but during a traffic spike latency explodes before new Pods are ready (5-min image pull + warmup).
scenarios.prompt: What are the fixes beyond 'scale faster'?
choices: Scale on leading signals (requests-per-second, queue depth), keep warm headroom (minReplicas buffer), shrink startup time (smaller images, pre-warming), and consider predictive/proactive scaling
Set maxReplicas higher — that fixes latency
HPA can't help — disable it
CPU is the only valid HPA metric
scenarios.why: Reactive CPU-based scaling lags spikes: by the time CPU rises, latency has already blown. Better: scale on the actual demand signal (RPS, queue length via custom metrics), maintain a warm buffer for spikes, cut cold-start time, and use VPA for right-sizing requests. KEDA extends this to event sources. Autoscaling complements capacity planning — it doesn't replace the baseline.
scenarios.hint: What signal rises BEFORE cpu does when traffic spikes?

scenarios.title: The queue is the warning
scenarios.situation: CPU looks fine (60%), but p99 latency tripled. You find the DB connection pool exhausted — requests queue for connections.
scenarios.prompt: What observability concept explains 'fine CPU, terrible latency'?
choices: Saturation — some resource (pool, queue, threads) is the bottleneck; USE method says check saturation, not just utilization
CPU is the only real bottleneck — the pool theory is wrong
Latency can't triple without CPU rising
Add more app servers — that fixes pool exhaustion
scenarios.why: Saturation (queued work waiting for a constrained resource) kills latency long before utilization looks scary — connection pools, thread pools, disk I/O queues, network buffers. The USE method: check Utilization, Saturation, and Errors for every resource. Instrument pool stats (in-use, queued, wait time) — queue depth is the leading indicator.
scenarios.hint: What does a request do when no DB connection is free?

scenarios.title: First game day
scenarios.situation: You want to run a chaos experiment (kill a zone) to validate failover. Leadership fears causing a real outage.
scenarios.prompt: How do you run it safely?
choices: Start tiny (one Pod in staging), define steady-state hypothesis + abort conditions, run in business hours with the team watching, expand blast radius gradually
Kill production on Friday night — real conditions or nothing
Chaos engineering is reckless — never do it
Run it secretly so nobody panics
scenarios.why: Disciplined chaos: hypothesis ('we believe failover completes in <60s'), minimal blast radius first, automated abort/rollback conditions, business-hours with observers, game-day format. It validates what you believe about resilience — most first experiments reveal the failover was broken. Expand from staging to prod, Pod to zone, over time. This is how 'hope' becomes 'evidence'.
scenarios.hint: What is the smallest experiment that still tests the hypothesis?

scenarios.title: The page that gained 2 MB
scenarios.situation: The checkout page's JS bundle grew from 300KB to 2.3MB over six months. Conversion dropped. Each team says 'our feature needed it.'
scenarios.prompt: What process prevents this drift?
choices: Performance budgets — CI-enforced limits (bundle size, LCP, TTI) that fail builds exceeding them, owned by the team
Ban JavaScript — the only fix
Performance is QA's job at release time
Budgets slow shipping — accept the bloat
scenarios.why: Performance budgets make speed a CI gate like tests: bundle-size limits, Core Web Vitals thresholds (LCP, INP, CLS), API p99 budgets — enforced per PR with clear ownership and an exception process. Without budgets, every local optimization ('just one more library') degrades the global experience. Measure in CI, guard the user experience.
scenarios.hint: What would have failed the PR that added the 2MB?

scenarios.title: The 2-minute spike vs 5-minute scaling
scenarios.situation: Flash-sale traffic spikes 10x for 2 minutes. Autoscaling takes 5 minutes to add capacity. The last sale saw 6 minutes of errors.
evidence: spike duration: ~2 min; scale-up latency: 5 min
6 min of 5xx during last flash sale
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct approach?
choices: Pre-provision (scheduled scale-up) for known flash sales; keep autoscaling for unknown variance — 5-min scaling can't catch a 2-min spike
Make autoscaling more aggressive (scale up faster)
Accept the errors; spikes are rare
Over-provision permanently at flash-sale levels
scenarios.hint: Can any reactive system respond to a spike shorter than its reaction time?
scenarios.why: Autoscaling reacts to load; a 2-minute spike is over before 5-minute scaling responds — physics, not tuning. Known events get scheduled pre-provisioning (scale up 15 min before, down after); autoscaling handles the unknown. Choice 2 can't beat the spike duration. Choice 3 accepts user-facing errors as policy. Choice 4 pays flash-sale capacity 24/7. Correct: pre-provision known peaks, autoscale the rest.

scenarios.title: Paved road, not dirt track
scenarios.situation: Every team builds its own CI pipeline, picks its own base images, and hand-rolls deploy scripts. Security findings and outages trace back to these snowflakes.
scenarios.prompt: What is the platform answer?
choices: Golden paths / paved roads — opinionated, supported defaults (templates, base images, pipelines) that are easy to adopt and hard to get wrong, with escape hatches
Ban all custom tooling — mandate one rigid pipeline
Let teams do anything — autonomy beats standards
Paved roads mean no choices at all
scenarios.why: Golden paths make the secure, reliable way the EASY way: templated services with baked-in scanning, logging, SLOs, and deploy pipelines. Teams can diverge (escape hatches exist) but then own the extra burden. Adoption is the metric — a paved road nobody uses is just documentation. This is the IDP's core product.
scenarios.hint: How do you make the right way also the easy way?

scenarios.title: Treating the platform as a product
scenarios.situation: The platform team ships features nobody uses and learns about pain from escalations. Developers call the platform 'the team that says no.'
scenarios.prompt: What changes when you run platform as a product?
choices: Developers become customers: research their workflows, measure adoption and time-to-first-deploy, publish a roadmap, and support the platform like a product
More features — volume wins users
Platforms shouldn't have users — they're infrastructure
Chargeback billing — money fixes adoption
scenarios.why: Platform-as-product: user research with dev teams, paved-road offerings with docs/SLAs, success metrics (adoption %, lead time, toil reduction), and a feedback loop (office hours, RFCs). The DORA metrics (deploy frequency, lead time, MTTR, change failure rate) measure whether the platform actually accelerates delivery. Mandates without empathy produce shadow platforms.
scenarios.hint: Who are the platform's users, and when did you last watch them work?

scenarios.title: Noisy neighbor on the platform
scenarios.situation: Team A's load test starves Team B's production workloads on the shared cluster. There are no quotas, no priority, no network policy.
scenarios.prompt: What are the multitenancy controls?
choices: Namespaces per tenant + ResourceQuotas/LimitRanges (compute fairness), NetworkPolicies (traffic isolation), PriorityClasses (preemption order), and RBAC scoping
One cluster per team — sharing is impossible
Trust teams to behave — controls are overhead
Quotas alone solve everything
scenarios.why: Shared-platform fairness is layered: namespaces scope identity/RBAC; ResourceQuota caps aggregates per tenant; LimitRange sets sane defaults; NetworkPolicy isolates traffic; PriorityClasses let prod preempt batch; node pools/taints separate noisy workloads physically. No single control covers all dimensions — that's why it's a stack.
scenarios.hint: Which control caps CPU, which isolates traffic, which decides who gets evicted first?

scenarios.title: Click-ops on the platform
scenarios.situation: Platform engineers provision tenant namespaces, quotas, and databases via console clicks and tickets. Nothing is auditable; reproducing an environment takes days.
scenarios.prompt: How does GitOps change platform operations?
choices: Every platform change becomes a declarative PR (tenant templates, quotas, addons) applied by automation — auditable, reviewable, reproducible, rollbackable
GitOps is for apps — platforms are special
Tickets are more auditable than git
Automation removes the need for review
scenarios.why: GitOps for platforms: tenant onboarding = PR against a template (namespace, quotas, network policies, RBAC); cluster addons managed by the same pull-based sync; everything in git history with reviewers. It turns tribal click-knowledge into code and makes 'rebuild the platform' a real disaster-recovery option instead of a fantasy.
scenarios.hint: What would 'recreate this tenant environment from scratch' require today?

scenarios.title: Guardrails, not gates
scenarios.situation: Security wants every deployment reviewed by a committee (2-week delay). Developers want to ship daily. Both cite real risks.
scenarios.prompt: What is the guardrails-over-gates approach?
choices: Automated policy checks (admission control, pipeline gates: image scanning, no root, signed images) that block only violations — fast by default, safe by construction
Remove all checks — speed wins
Keep the committee — safety requires humans
Automated checks are theater — committees catch everything
scenarios.why: Guardrails encode policy as code: OPA/Kyverno admission policies (require non-root, approved registries, resource limits), pipeline checks (CVE scanning, SAST) — evaluated in seconds on every deploy. Gates (human committees) become the exception for genuinely novel risks. Developers ship fast within safe boundaries; security gets continuous enforcement instead of sampled reviews.
scenarios.hint: What enforces the policy on every deploy without a meeting?

scenarios.title: The team that owns everything
scenarios.situation: One team owns the Kubernetes platform, the CI system, the databases, the network, and on-call for all of it. They're drowning; nothing improves.
scenarios.prompt: What does Team Topologies say about this?
choices: Cognitive load is finite — split into focused teams (platform team as enabling/complicated-subsystem), with clear ownership boundaries and thinnest viable interfaces
Hire more people into the same team — scale solves load
One team owning everything is ideal — no handoffs
Outsource it all — ownership is the problem
scenarios.why: Team Topologies: teams have finite cognitive load; exceeding it means nothing gets done well. Patterns: stream-aligned teams (own a product slice end-to-end), platform teams (reduce others' load via self-service), enabling teams (temporary coaching). The fix isn't headcount into one mega-team — it's boundaries that keep each team's load sustainable.
scenarios.hint: Can one team deeply understand five complex domains at once?

scenarios.title: The platform nobody uses
scenarios.situation: The platform team built a full PaaS. Six months later, 3 of 40 teams use it; the rest maintain their own pipelines.
evidence: 'too hard to migrate', 'doesn't support our workflow', 'we didn't know it existed'
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response?
choices: Treat it as a product failure: interview teams, fix onboarding (golden-path migration tooling), support the missing workflows, market the wins — measure adoption as the KPI
Mandate migration by executive order
Add more features to the platform
Declare the holdouts non-compliant
scenarios.hint: Is 99.99% uptime the right KPI for a platform with 7% adoption?
scenarios.why: 99.99% uptime with 7% adoption is a failed product — the survey says why: migration friction, workflow gaps, awareness. Mandates (choice 2/4) breed resentment and shadow workarounds; more features (choice 3) don't fix onboarding. The product response — user interviews, paved-road migration, workflow coverage, adoption KPI — addresses the actual blockers. Correct: product discipline, adoption as the metric.

scenarios.title: Is this toil?
scenarios.situation: Four candidates: (a) manually provisioning VMs from tickets, (b) designing a new sharding scheme, (c) copy-pasting dashboard JSON per service, (d) debugging a novel cascading failure.
scenarios.prompt: Which are toil, by the SRE definition?
choices: (a) and (c) — manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, no enduring value, scaling linearly with service growth
(b) and (d) — engineering work is toil
All four — all operational work is toil
None — toil is just a synonym for hard work
scenarios.why: Toil's criteria: manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical (not strategic), no enduring value, and growing with the service (O(n)). Provisioning tickets and dashboard copy-paste qualify; novel design and unprecedented debugging are engineering. The SRE prescription: cap toil at 50% of time and systematically automate the rest away.
scenarios.hint: Which tasks would still exist in the same form after automation?

scenarios.title: The 50% rule
scenarios.situation: Your team spends 80% of its time on toil (manual deploys, ticket-driven ops). Feature teams demand more operational support.
scenarios.prompt: What does the SRE model prescribe?
choices: Cap toil at 50%: if exceeded, halt feature/ops intake and invest in automation until toil drops — toil is the signal, not the job
Hire more people to do the toil — it's the job
Work longer hours — 80% is normal
Stop measuring — the number causes anxiety
scenarios.why: Google's SRE rule: max 50% of anyone's time on toil; beyond that the team must spend the surplus eliminating toil (automation, self-service) even at the cost of feature velocity. It's a forcing function: without the cap, toil grows unboundedly and engineering becomes pure operations. Measure toil honestly (surveys/time tracking) to enforce it.
scenarios.hint: What happens to engineering capacity if toil grows unchecked?

scenarios.title: From runbook to self-service
scenarios.situation: The 'scale up the workers' runbook is 40 manual steps run 3x/week. You've automated it into a script — but only you can run it safely.
scenarios.prompt: What is the progression from script to toil elimination?
choices: Docs → script → hardened automation (guardrails, dry-run) → self-service (ChatOps/portal button) → autonomous (autoscaling) — each step removes human involvement
The script is enough — stop there
Delete the runbook — scripts replace docs
Automation increases toil — avoid it
scenarios.why: The toil-elimination ladder: document (runbook), script (repeatable), automate with safety (idempotent, dry-run, rollback), self-service (anyone can trigger safely via portal/ChatOps), autonomous (system does it — autoscaling). Each rung reduces human touch. A script only you can run is step 2 of 5 — keep climbing until the toil is gone, not just faster.
scenarios.hint: Who can safely run your script today — and who should be able to?

scenarios.title: The automation that made it worse
scenarios.situation: An auto-remediation script restarts 'unhealthy' services — but its health check was wrong, so it restart-looped the entire fleet during a partial outage, amplifying it.
scenarios.prompt: What safety properties must automation have?
choices: Blast-radius limits (canary/percentage rollouts), dry-run modes, automatic abort on unexpected signals, idempotency, and human override — automation needs circuit breakers too
Automation should never touch production — keep it advisory
More automation — the script just needed to be faster
Delete the health check — checks cause the problem
scenarios.why: Automation amplifies both good and bad: unsafe automation fails at machine speed. Required properties: limited blast radius (percentage/canary), dry-run/preview, abort conditions (stop if the world looks weird), idempotency (safe to rerun), observability (what did it do and why), and a big red button. Auto-remediation earns trust gradually — start advisory, then semi-auto, then auto with tight bounds.
scenarios.hint: What stops the script when its assumptions are wrong?

scenarios.title: Proving toil is shrinking
scenarios.situation: Leadership asks 'is the automation investment working?' You need evidence that toil is actually decreasing.
scenarios.prompt: How do you measure toil reduction?
choices: Track toil hours (surveys/time logs), ticket volumes and MTTR for automated workflows, manual intervention counts, and deployment lead times — trends, not vanity totals
Count lines of automation code — more code means less toil
Ask the team vibes — measurement is overhead
Toil can't be measured — it's subjective
scenarios.why: Measure the work, not the code: % time on toil (Google's metric), tickets/requests per week for automated flows, manual steps per deploy, MTTR before/after runbook automation, lead time. Trends over quarters prove the investment. Vanity metrics (scripts written, dashboards built) don't — a script nobody uses is not toil reduction.
scenarios.hint: What would change in the team's week if toil truly shrank?

scenarios.title: Protecting engineering time
scenarios.situation: Every sprint, 'urgent' operational requests consume the engineering backlog. The team hasn't shipped a reliability improvement in 6 months.
scenarios.prompt: What structural fix protects project work?
choices: Explicit capacity split (e.g., 50% toil cap, protected project time), an ops rotation absorbing interrupts, and saying no to non-urgent requests with a queue
Work weekends — capacity is elastic
Do project work 'when there's time' — it appears eventually
Hire contractors for projects — the team does ops
scenarios.why: Interrupt-driven teams need structure: an on-call/ops rotation takes the interrupts (shielding the rest), project time is calendar-protected, and incoming requests go through triage (urgent vs queue). Without this, the urgent always eats the important — and reliability work, which prevents future interrupts, never happens. The toil budget and the rotation are the two mechanisms.
scenarios.hint: Who handles this week's interrupts while others do project work?

choices: Cap toil (Google's SRE book sets the bar at 50% max, aiming lower), then systematically automate the toil away — adding headcount to a toil-heavy team just scales the toil linearly instead of eliminating it
Hire two more SREs; toil is normal operations work
Outsource the toil to a managed services vendor and keep headcount flat
Accept 60% toil; SRE is mostly operations anyway
scenarios.hint: If traffic doubles, what happens to this toil — and what happens to it if you automate it instead?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct SRE response before hiring?
scenarios.situation: The SRE team spends 60% of its time on manual toil: hand-running database migrations, manually rotating certs, clicking through cloud consoles to provision. They ask for headcount.
scenarios.title: Toil Audit
scenarios.why: Toil is the work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, and devoid of enduring value — and it scales with service growth, so hiring into it is a treadmill. The SRE discipline: measure toil, cap it, and spend the freed engineering time automating it away. Each automation permanently reduces the toil fraction; each hire without automation just adds capacity for more toil.

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Sre Platform as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The SLIs/SLOs Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that SLIs/SLOs is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in SLIs/SLOs?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — SLIs/SLOs issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — SLIs/SLOs is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is SLIs/SLOs supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any SLIs/SLOs failure in Sre Platform.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
evidence: All SLIs/SLOs components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: The Incident Response Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Incident Response is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Incident Response?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Incident Response issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Incident Response is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Incident Response supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Incident Response failure in Sre Platform.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Incident Response
evidence: All Incident Response components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

domains.name: Start Here: How to Master This Bootcamp
domains.description: Orientation, study strategy, and what SRE interviews and assessments actually test.

domains.name: Chaos Engineering & Resilience Testing
domains.description: Hypothesis-driven failure injection, blast-radius control, game days, and chaos in CI/CD.

scenarios.title: First chaos experiment
scenarios.situation: Leadership approved chaos engineering. The team wants to start with 'kill a production region' to prove value.
evidence: experiment 1: terminate all prod instances in us-east
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct starting point?
choices: Start small and staged: kill single pods in staging with a written hypothesis and abort conditions; graduate scope only after clean passes
Run the region kill — big bang proves the most
Skip to production single-AZ after one staging test
Do tabletop exercises instead of real injection
scenarios.hint: What validates the safety process before the blast radius grows?
scenarios.why: Chaos without safety progression is just causing outages: untested runbooks + region-scale fault = uncontained incident. The discipline is hypothesis → small blast radius → abort conditions → graduated scope. Staging pod-kills validate the tooling and process; production comes later. Choice 2 is reckless. Choice 3 skips grades. Choice 4 (tabletops only) never tests reality. Correct: staged progression from small/safe.

scenarios.title: Hypothesis vs havoc
scenarios.situation: An engineer runs weekly 'chaos Fridays' killing random pods. Nothing is written down; findings aren't tracked.
evidence: random pod kills, no hypothesis, no steady-state definition
scenarios.prompt: What needs to change?
choices: Every experiment gets a written card: steady-state, hypothesis, blast radius, abort conditions — and results feed the backlog
Kill more interesting things (databases, DNS)
Run chaos daily instead of weekly
Stop chaos; it clearly doesn't work here
scenarios.hint: After a random pod kill, what did the team learn?
scenarios.why: Without a hypothesis there's nothing to learn: random kills that the system survives teach nothing, and ones it doesn't survive are just outages. The experiment card converts breaking into learning — steady-state defines 'normal', the hypothesis states the belief, results confirm or refute it, and refutations become backlog items. Choices 2/3 scale up the havoc without adding learning. Choice 4 blames the practice for the missing discipline. Correct: hypothesis-driven cards with tracked outcomes.

scenarios.title: The experiment that became an incident
scenarios.situation: A latency-injection experiment had no abort hook. Steady state broke at minute 3; the engineer noticed at minute 25. Users were affected.
evidence: fault injected 10:00; errors > 5% from 10:03; noticed 10:25; halted 10:27
no automated abort; manual monitoring only
scenarios.prompt: What is the required safeguard?
choices: Automated abort hooks on steady-state deviation (errors > threshold for N min → auto-halt) plus a manual kill switch — at least two independent abort paths
Shorter experiments
More careful engineers watching dashboards
Only run experiments at 3am when traffic is low
scenarios.hint: What stops the experiment when the human isn't watching?
scenarios.why: Manual monitoring is a single point of failure — attention lapses, and 22 minutes of user impact resulted. Automated abort on the same SLI the hypothesis references stops the experiment the moment steady state breaks; the manual kill switch is the backup. Choice 2 helps but doesn't bound damage. Choice 3 is the 'be more careful' anti-pattern. Choice 4 reduces blast radius by timing but keeps the missing safeguard. Correct: automated abort + manual kill switch.

scenarios.title: Game day with no debrief
scenarios.situation: The team ran an AZ-failure game day. It went well, everyone had fun, and no action items were recorded.
evidence: AZ failover game day: recovered in 18 min
no debrief held; no action items
scenarios.prompt: What was missing?
choices: The debrief: structured review of surprises and gaps, producing tracked action items — the debrief is the product of the game day
A harder scenario next time
More participants
Longer game day duration
scenarios.hint: What is the durable output of a game day?
scenarios.why: The value of a game day isn't the rehearsal — it's the surprises surfaced ('the runbook's third step is wrong', 'we didn't know who decides failback'). Without a debrief capturing them as tracked action items, the same surprises recur in the real incident. Choices 2/3/4 optimize the event, not the learning. Correct: mandatory debrief with action items.

scenarios.title: Dependency failure drill
scenarios.situation: Checkout depends on a fraud-check API. Nobody has tested what happens when fraud-check is slow or down.
scenarios.prompt: What experiment do you design?
choices: Inject latency then full failure into fraud-check in staging: hypothesis is that timeouts + fallback (or graceful degradation) keep checkout serving
Kill checkout pods to test recovery
Load-test fraud-check to its limit
Add a second fraud-check vendor
scenarios.hint: Which architectural bet is currently untested?
scenarios.why: The architectural bet is 'checkout survives fraud-check degradation' — currently untested, and the 2s synchronous call with no fallback suggests the bet is wrong. Fault injection directly tests it: latency first (does p99 blow up?), then failure (does checkout collapse?). Choice 1's result dictates the fix (timeouts, circuit breaker, fallback). Choices 2/3 test the wrong thing. Choice 4 (second vendor) is a possible fix, but you experiment first to know what needs fixing. Correct: dependency fault injection.

scenarios.title: Resilience gate in the pipeline
scenarios.situation: A deploy removed a retry wrapper; checkout started failing when inventory was slow. Code review missed it; tests didn't cover it.
evidence: PR removed retry logic; no test asserted resilience
30 min of checkout errors during inventory slowness
scenarios.prompt: What systemic fix prevents recurrence?
choices: A chaos gate in CI: inject dependency latency/failure during integration tests and assert graceful degradation — the PR fails if resilience regresses
More careful code reviews
A wiki page on retry best practices
Ban removing retry logic
scenarios.hint: What would have caught this PR automatically?
scenarios.why: Reviews and wiki pages don't catch what tests don't assert. A CI chaos gate makes resilience a build property: every PR is tested against dependency failure, and regressions fail the build in minutes. Choice 2/3 rely on human vigilance. Choice 4 is unenforceable. Correct: automated resilience gate in the pipeline.

scenarios.title: Unscoped experiment
scenarios.situation: An experiment configured 'kill 30% of pods' without a namespace selector ran against the production cluster instead of staging.
evidence: target: '30% of pods' — no cluster/namespace specified
production checkout pods killed; 12 min incident
scenarios.prompt: What controls prevent this?
choices: Mandatory scoping (cluster + namespace selectors), environment separation (separate chaos tooling/credentials per env), and config review before run
Fewer chaos experiments
Only run chaos in staging forever
Blame the engineer who ran it
scenarios.hint: What in the config allowed prod to be targeted?
scenarios.why: The fault wasn't wrong — the targeting was. Mandatory scoping fields, separate credentials per environment (staging chaos tooling physically cannot address prod), and a second pair of eyes on the config are the systemic fixes. Choice 2/3 abandon the practice. Choice 4 is blame culture. Correct: scoping + environment separation + review.

domains.name: Multi-Region & Disaster Recovery
domains.description: Active-active vs active-passive, replication, traffic steering, failover drills, RTO/RPO.

scenarios.title: Choosing the DR topology
scenarios.situation: The business requires checkout RTO 15 min, RPO 1 min. The team proposes active-passive with monthly failover drills.
evidence: active-passive, async replication (lag ~2 min), monthly drills
scenarios.prompt: Does the proposal meet the requirements?
choices: No: async lag (~2 min) already exceeds the 1-min RPO, and 15-min RTO needs automated, well-drilled failover — this needs sync replication (or single-writer shards) and more frequent drills
Yes, active-passive with monthly drills is sufficient
Yes, but switch to weekly drills
No — only active-active can do 15-min RTO
scenarios.hint: What is the RPO floor set by the replication lag?
scenarios.why: Two gaps: the 2-minute replication lag violates RPO 1 min by itself (need sync replication or bounded-lag single-writer), and monthly drills won't sustain 15-minute RTOs (need automation + frequent drills). Choice 2/3 accept the RPO violation. Choice 4 overstates — well-automated active-passive can hit 15-min RTO. Correct: fix replication for RPO, automate + drill frequently for RTO.

scenarios.title: Split-brain during partition
scenarios.situation: A network partition isolated us-east. Both regions accepted writes for 20 minutes. Now there are conflicting orders with the same IDs.
evidence: multi-writer, no fencing, no conflict strategy
scenarios.prompt: What should the design have included?
choices: Quorum/fencing (only the majority partition writes) or single-writer-per-shard; plus a defined conflict-resolution strategy for anything multi-writer
Faster partition repair
Manual reconciliation after every partition
Bigger network pipes
scenarios.hint: What stops the minority partition from accepting writes?
scenarios.why: Without fencing, a partition creates two divergent truths — reconciliation is then manual and lossy. Quorum (minority partition stops writing) or single-writer-per-shard (writers never conflict) prevents divergence structurally; where multi-writer is unavoidable, a defined resolution strategy (LWW/CRDT) bounds the damage. Choice 2/4 don't prevent dual-writes. Choice 3 accepts regular data corruption as operations. Correct: fencing/quorum or single-writer design.

scenarios.title: DNS failover too slow
scenarios.situation: Region failover relies on DNS with 5-min TTL. During the last failover, 40% of clients kept hitting the dead region for 30+ minutes.
evidence: 40% of traffic on dead region 30 min after cutover
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct fix?
choices: Anycast IPs with health-checked load balancing for fast steering; keep DNS as backup, not the primary mechanism
Lower TTL to 10 seconds
Tell customers to flush DNS
Add more DNS providers
scenarios.hint: Who actually honors your TTL?
scenarios.why: Clients and resolvers ignore TTLs routinely — 30 minutes of stale traffic proves it. Anycast moves traffic at the routing layer in seconds-to-minutes regardless of client DNS behavior. Choice 2 helps marginally but doesn't fix non-compliant resolvers. Choice 3/4 are not real solutions. Correct: anycast + health checks as the steering mechanism.

scenarios.title: Failover worked; failback didn't
scenarios.situation: The team failed over to us-west cleanly. Failing back to us-east corrupted data: replication had been one-directional and nobody re-synced.
evidence: data loss on return to primary
scenarios.prompt: What is the lesson?
choices: Drill the full cycle including failback: re-establish replication in reverse, verify sync, then shift traffic — failback is a second failover, not an undo
Never fail back; stay in us-west
Fail back faster next time
Use bidirectional replication always
scenarios.hint: What happened to the writes made in us-west during the outage?
scenarios.why: Failback is not 'undo' — during the outage, us-west accumulated writes that us-east lacks. Returning without re-syncing (reverse replication, verification) discards them. The drill must cover the full cycle: over, back, verified. Choice 2 avoids the problem by abandoning the primary. Choice 3 speeds up the data loss. Choice 4 (always bidirectional) adds conflict complexity for a drill problem. Correct: test and procedure-ize failback.

scenarios.title: Replication lag alert nobody owns
scenarios.situation: Replication lag hit 45 minutes last night. No alert fired; the morning report just shows stale data in the secondary region.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct fix?
choices: Alert on replication lag with thresholds tied to RPO (warn at 50% of RPO, page near 100%), owned by the data team, with a runbook
Increase replication bandwidth
Accept lag as normal for async replication
Fail over to the secondary to 'catch up'
scenarios.hint: What does 45 minutes of lag mean for your stated RPO?
scenarios.why: Lag is the RPO made visible — unmonitored lag means the RPO is a fiction. Thresholds derive from the RPO (warn at half, page near full), with an owner and runbook. Choice 2 may help but doesn't detect. Choice 3 accepts unbounded staleness. Choice 4 is nonsense — failing over to a 45-min-stale replica. Correct: RPO-derived lag alerting with ownership.

scenarios.title: One DR plan for everything
scenarios.situation: The company applies the same DR design (active-active, sync replication) to checkout, the internal wiki, and the staging environment.
evidence: wiki RTO could be 24h; nobody asked
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct approach?
choices: Tier by RTO/RPO: Tier 0 (checkout) gets the expensive design; Tier 2 (wiki) gets backups; each tier's design justified by signed-off numbers
Keep uniform DR — simplicity is worth it
Drop DR for everything except checkout
Move the wiki to active-active too, for consistency
scenarios.hint: What RTO does the wiki actually need — and what does its DR cost?
scenarios.why: Uniform gold-plating burns 3x spend protecting a wiki nobody needs in 15 minutes. Tiering matches cost to requirement: expensive designs only where the business signed off on tight RTO/RPO. Choice 2 pays triple for uniformity. Choice 3 swings to zero protection without analysis. Choice 4 doubles down. Correct: tiered DR from written requirements.

scenarios.title: Drill without measurements
scenarios.situation: The team 'successfully' failed over last quarter. Nobody recorded how long it took or how much data was lost.
evidence: 'failover successful' — no timings, no data-loss figure
RTO 15 min, RPO 1 min (unstated whether met)
scenarios.prompt: What is missing?
choices: Measured RTO/RPO achieved vs targets, plus a surprise log feeding action items — a drill without measurements can't prove the targets
A bigger drill scope
More frequent drills
Executive attendance
scenarios.hint: How do you know the 15-min RTO was met?
scenarios.why: 'Successful' without numbers is theater: did it take 12 minutes or 47? Was data loss 30 seconds or 10 minutes? The scorecard (achieved RTO/RPO vs target, surprises → actions) is what justifies confidence — or exposes the gap. Choices 2/3/4 improve the event, not the evidence. Correct: measure every drill against the targets.

domains.name: Cost Optimization for Reliable Systems
domains.description: Cost visibility, rightsizing, autoscaling economics, spot capacity, SLO-aware tradeoffs.

scenarios.title: The unattributable bill
scenarios.situation: The cloud bill grew 40% in a quarter. 60% of resources are untagged; nobody knows which team owns the growth.
scenarios.prompt: What is the first step?
choices: Enforce tagging (team/service/environment) via policy — block untagged provisioning — then attribute and showback per team
Negotiate a bigger discount with the provider
Cut 20% of instances arbitrarily
Move to a cheaper provider
scenarios.hint: Who can cut spend they can't see?
scenarios.why: Unattributable spend can't be optimized — you can't ask a team to cut what you can't show them. Tagging enforcement (policy-as-code blocking untagged deploys) plus showback reports creates accountability; the actual waste reveals itself once visible. Choices 2/4 change pricing, not behavior. Choice 3 cuts blind. Correct: attribute first, then optimize.

scenarios.title: Rightsizing the over-provisioned fleet
scenarios.situation: A service requests 8 CPU / 32GB per pod; p95 usage over 90 days is 1.2 CPU / 4GB. 200 pods.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct action?
choices: Rightsize toward measured p95 plus buffer (e.g., 2 CPU / 8 GB), roll out gradually with monitoring, and re-check after the change
Leave it — headroom is good
Cut to exactly p95 (1.2 CPU / 4 GB)
Double the pods and halve the size
scenarios.hint: What does the 90-day p95 tell you about the other 85% of allocated capacity?
scenarios.why: The fleet runs at ~15% of request — clear waste. Sizing to p95 + buffer keeps peaks safe while reclaiming most of the waste; gradual rollout with monitoring catches the unexpected. Choice 2 defends 6x over-provisioning as 'headroom'. Choice 3 removes all buffer — the next p99.9 spike OOMs. Choice 4 is churn without analysis. Correct: measured rightsizing with buffer, rolled out safely.

scenarios.title: Idle non-prod environments
scenarios.situation: 40 dev environments run 24/7 at full size. Usage logs show activity 9am-6pm weekdays only.
scenarios.prompt: What is the highest-ROI move?
choices: Scheduled scale-to-zero: nights and weekends off, auto-up on first morning access — ~73% compute savings with zero performance risk
Rightsize each environment
Move dev to spot instances
Ask developers to shut down manually
scenarios.hint: What fraction of the week is anyone using these environments?
scenarios.why: The environments sit idle 73% of the week — scheduled shutdown captures nearly three-quarters of the cost with no architectural risk and no performance tradeoff. Rightsizing (choice 2) trims the active 27%, a smaller win. Spot (choice 3) helps but keeps idle spend. Manual shutdown (choice 4) never happens consistently. Correct: automated schedule.

scenarios.title: Spot for the stateful singleton
scenarios.situation: To save money, the team moved the primary database to spot VMs. Last night a reclamation caused 40 minutes of downtime.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct policy?
choices: Spot for interruptible workloads (stateless tiers, batch, CI); stateful singletons and primaries stay on on-demand/reserved
Add faster failover so reclamations don't hurt
Use spot but with diversfied instance types
Accept the risk; the savings are worth it
scenarios.hint: What does the spot contract promise — and can a primary DB accept it?
scenarios.why: Spot's contract is 'we can take this back with notice' — a primary database cannot tolerate that. The savings on the DB are dwarfed by 40 minutes of outage. Spot belongs on stateless/burst/batch capacity with graceful handling; the data layer stays on stable capacity. Choices 2/3 mitigate but don't fix the category error. Choice 4 prices the outage at zero. Correct: workload-appropriate placement.

scenarios.title: Totals vs unit economics
scenarios.situation: The bill is flat at $200k/mo while traffic doubled. Finance wants a 20% cut; engineering says 'we're already efficient'.
scenarios.prompt: How do you resolve the debate?
choices: Unit economics: cost per 1k requests halved as traffic doubled — efficiency is improving; a blind 20% cut risks the SLOs achieving it
Cut 20% across the board as finance asks
Refuse any cuts; reliability is priceless
Cut the monitoring budget (it's 'overhead')
scenarios.hint: What happened to cost per request while the total stayed flat?
scenarios.why: Flat totals with doubled traffic means unit cost halved — the team is genuinely efficient, and blind cuts would likely breach the SLOs that efficiency supports. Unit economics reframes the conversation from 'spend less' to 'spend per unit', and any cut proposal must name which reliability tier it degrades. Choice 2/4 cut blind. Choice 3 refuses engagement. Correct: decide on unit economics with SLO impact explicit.

scenarios.title: Cheapest path that keeps the SLO
scenarios.situation: Two designs both meet the 99.9% SLO: A costs $30k/mo (multi-AZ, sync), B costs $12k/mo (multi-AZ, async + tested failover).
scenarios.prompt: Which do you choose and why?
choices: B: both meet the SLO, so the cheaper design wins — reliability beyond the SLO has no user-visible value; document the choice and the failover drill cadence
A: more reliability is always better
A: sync is simpler to reason about
B, but skip the drills to save more
scenarios.hint: What do users feel differently between A and B?
scenarios.why: The SLO is the contract: once met, extra nines are invisible to users but very visible on the bill. B meets the SLO at 40% of the cost — the rational choice, with the drill cadence as the load-bearing assumption (documented and scheduled). Choice 2/3 pay $18k/mo for nothing users feel. Choice 4 removes the assumption B depends on. Correct: cheapest SLO-meeting design, with its assumptions explicit.

scenarios.title: Error budget as spending permission
scenarios.situation: Off-peak, checkout runs 12 replicas for a 99.95% SLO; the error budget is 90% full. Traffic is 10% of peak.
scenarios.prompt: Is the proposal sound?
choices: Yes, if modeled: 6 replicas still meet the SLO at 10% traffic with headroom, and the full budget gives room to revert — a deliberate, reversible tradeoff
No — never reduce reliability spending
Yes — cut to 2 replicas, budget is full
No — replica count must never change
scenarios.hint: What is a full error budget for, if not deliberate tradeoffs?
scenarios.why: A full error budget is permission to take measured risks: the proposal is sound if the math holds (6 replicas × headroom ≥ 10% traffic peaks) and it's reversible (scale back up on budget burn). Choice 2 treats all reliability spend as sacred. Choice 3 skips the modeling — 2 replicas has no headroom. Choice 4 freezes operations. Correct: modeled, reversible, budget-aware tradeoff.

domains.name: Progressive Delivery & Safe Rollouts
domains.description: Canary analysis, blue-green, feature flags, automated rollback, deployment freezes.

scenarios.title: Canary with no analysis
scenarios.situation: Deploys shift 5% traffic to the new version for 30 minutes while someone 'watches the dashboard', then proceed. A bad deploy still reached 100% last week.
evidence: regression missed; full rollout of bad version
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Automated analysis: metric comparisons (error rate, p99) vs baseline with pass/fail thresholds and auto-rollback — humans don't reliably spot 0.2% regressions
Longer canary (2 hours)
Bigger canary (25%)
More experienced dashboard watchers
scenarios.hint: Can a human reliably see a 0.2% regression at 5% traffic?
scenarios.why: Humans watching dashboards miss slow-burn regressions — 0.2% error increases don't look alarming at 5% traffic. Automated statistical comparison against baseline catches what eyes miss, and auto-rollback removes the hesitation. Longer/bigger (choices 2/3) without analysis just exposes more users to the bad version. Choice 4 doesn't fix human pattern-matching limits. Correct: automated analysis with auto-rollback.

scenarios.title: The flag with no owner
scenarios.situation: The codebase has 340 feature flags. Nobody knows which are safe to remove; a cleanup attempt broke checkout (a 'dead' flag was still load-bearing).
evidence: 340 flags; 60% older than a year; owners unknown
scenarios.prompt: What is the systemic fix?
choices: Flag lifecycle policy: every flag gets an owner + expiry date at creation; quarterly audits; removal via the same canary process as code changes
Delete all flags older than a year
Freeze new flag creation
Move flags to config files
scenarios.hint: What distinguishes a live flag from a dead one today?
scenarios.why: The incident came from missing lifecycle, not from flags themselves: no owner, no expiry, removal without process. The policy makes flags temporary by default (owner + expiry at creation), audits catch stragglers, and removal goes through canary like any change. Choice 2 repeats the incident at scale. Choice 3 blocks a legitimate tool. Choice 4 changes the storage, not the lifecycle. Correct: lifecycle policy with ownership and expiry.

scenarios.title: Rollback that didn't
scenarios.situation: During an incident the team 'rolled back' the deploy, but errors continued: the bad config flag stayed at its new value.
evidence: code rolled back to 1.4.1; flag new_checkout stayed true
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct rollback design?
choices: Rollback the whole unit — code + config + flags — as one atomic operation; verify error budget recovers after
Roll back code faster next time
Never use flags with deploys
Roll forward with a fix instead
scenarios.hint: Which combinations of code+flag were ever tested together?
scenarios.why: The deploy's unit was code+config+flag; rolling back only code left the system in a state that never existed in testing (old code + new flag). Atomic rollback of the full unit restores a known-good combination. Choice 2 speeds up the partial fix. Choice 3 discards flags' value. Choice 4 (roll forward) is legitimate when a fix is ready in minutes, but the rollback design must still be atomic for when it isn't. Correct: whole-unit rollback.

scenarios.title: The freeze everyone violates
scenarios.situation: A holiday deploy freeze exists 'on paper'. Three teams deployed during it last year; one caused the holiday outage.
scenarios.prompt: What makes the freeze real?
choices: Narrow scope (risky changes only), a defined emergency exception path, and pipeline enforcement that blocks prod deploys during the window
Stricter emails from leadership
Freezing all changes including safe ones
Punishing violators
scenarios.hint: Why did teams feel they needed to violate it?
scenarios.why: Email freezes leak because they're unenforced and overbroad. The working design: freeze only risky changes (so teams don't need to violate it for safe work), give emergencies a legitimate path (approval + extra validation), and enforce in the pipeline (the deploy job refuses). Choices 2/4 are theater. Choice 3 makes violations more likely, not fewer. Correct: scoped + exception path + automated enforcement.

scenarios.title: Rolling deploy meets breaking change
scenarios.situation: A rolling deploy shipped v2 API while v1 instances still served. v2 clients hit v1 instances and errored for 20 minutes.
evidence: rolling: v1 and v2 coexisted 20 min
scenarios.prompt: What is the required discipline?
choices: Backward/forward compatibility during coexistence: v2 clients must tolerate v1 responses (or traffic must pin versions); contract tested in CI
Deploy faster so coexistence is shorter
Switch to blue-green
Deploy at 3am when traffic is low
scenarios.hint: What versions coexist during a rolling deploy — and what must hold between them?
scenarios.why: Rolling deploys guarantee version coexistence — the system must be designed for it. v2 clients need to handle v1 responses (or the router pins clients to matching versions); CI should test the mixed-version matrix. Choice 2 shortens but doesn't eliminate the window. Choice 3 changes strategy without fixing the contract gap (blue-green has its own coexistence issues with state). Choice 4 hides it. Correct: version-tolerant contracts, tested.

scenarios.title: No kill switch on the risky launch
scenarios.situation: A new recommendation engine launched to 100% with no flag. It degraded checkout latency; the only mitigation was a full rollback (25 min).
evidence: 100% rollout, no flag, no gradual ramp
scenarios.prompt: What should the launch have included?
choices: A kill switch (feature flag) plus gradual rollout: instant disable in seconds when latency degraded, instead of a 25-min rollback
More load testing before launch
A faster rollback pipeline
Launching at low-traffic hours
scenarios.hint: How long should 'turn off the new thing' take?
scenarios.why: The 25-minute mitigation was the real failure: with a kill switch, the team disables the feature in seconds and investigates calmly. Gradual rollout would have limited the blast radius to a small % first. Choices 2/4 reduce risk but don't bound mitigation time. Choice 3 helps but rollback will always be slower than a flag flip. Correct: flag-gated gradual launch with kill switch.

scenarios.title: Deploy vs migration ordering
scenarios.situation: A deploy ran a migration dropping a column the old code still reads. During the rolling deploy, old instances crashed.
evidence: DROP COLUMN email in the same deploy as code removal
old instances queried the dropped column → crashes
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe sequence?
choices: Expand/contract: deploy code that doesn't need the column → migrate/drop → deploy cleanup; each step independently safe and reversible
Run migrations before deploys, always
Run migrations after deploys, always
Take downtime for schema changes
scenarios.hint: Which code versions are live when the column disappears?
scenarios.why: The crash came from ordering: schema changed while old code was live. Expand/contract separates the phases so old code never sees a schema it can't handle and new code never needs a column that's gone — each step deployable and reversible alone. 'Migrations first' (choice 2) breaks old code the same way; 'after' (choice 3) breaks new code instead. Downtime (choice 4) is sometimes acceptable but unnecessary here. Correct: expand/contract sequencing.

domains.name: Change Safety & Configuration Management
domains.description: Safe config changes, schema migrations, change review, and blast-radius control.

scenarios.title: The 'just config' outage
scenarios.situation: An engineer hand-edited a timeout value in production ('just config, no review needed'). The value had a wrong unit; checkout timed out fleet-wide.
evidence: hand-edited prod config: timeout 5000 (ms assumed, s parsed)
scenarios.prompt: What is the systemic fix?
